//: BASELINE permissions — applied by every install.sh run.
This file only ever NARROWS what Claude may do. `deny` and `ask` entries are
UNIONED into your existing settings; nothing is removed, and `allow` and
defaultMode are deliberately absent so Claude Code's normal prompting stays
exactly as it is. Installing this cannot make your setup more permissive.
You can stop specific `ask` rules being re-added with
`permissions.baseline_opt_out` in your config (see config.example.json).
`deny` blocks a path outright. `ask` forces a confirmation prompt even when a
broader allow rule would otherwise cover the command. Two kinds of thing live
here, and they are here for different reasons.
OUTWARD-FACING: pushing, opening or merging a PR, cutting a release,
publishing a package. Those are decisions, not execution steps.
LOCALLY DESTRUCTIVE: git reset, git clean, git stash drop/clear. These
destroy work that has never been pushed anywhere — no reflog entry for the
working tree, no remote, no second copy — and claude-danger-guard has no
rule for the family, so these `ask` rules are the only thing that stops
one before it runs. They prompt; they do not block.
The git rules are written broadly on purpose. A prefix rule cannot see flag
ORDER, so `Bash(git reset --hard *)` would miss `git reset -q --hard`, which
is the more common real spelling. These commands are rare in ordinary work,
so the broad forms prompt far less often than the git push rule beside them.
Rules DO see inside a compound command (a deny rule fires on a command four
links deep in an && chain, on semicolon-separated commands, and inside a for
loop body), so `cd /repo && git reset --hard` is covered.
Add your own secrets directory to `deny` if you keep one (service-account
JSON, exported credentials, personal data). Paths support globs and ~.
Not included on purpose: Read(**/.env). It would be defensible, but .env files
are read legitimately often enough that a blanket deny becomes an obstacle you
route around, and a rule you route around protects nothing. Deny the specific
directories that actually hold your credentials instead.
